subsection: 3. Wilhelm II and Weltpolitik; case study: the naval policy of Wilhelm II, 1890–1914

notes.h: Background: the Reich, Bismarck and Britain's navy
notes.b: To judge Wilhelm II's policies you need to know what he inherited: a constitution that gave the Kaiser great power, a cautious foreign policy that he rejected, and a world in which Britain ruled the seas.
points: Under the 1871 constitution the Kaiser appointed and dismissed the Chancellor, was supreme commander of the armed forces and directed foreign policy, so a strong-willed Kaiser could in theory rule personally.

The Reichstag (the elected parliament, chosen by universal male suffrage) voted laws and the budget, so every Navy Law and every naval tax needed a Reichstag majority, however much the Kaiser wanted a fleet.

Bismarck called Germany a satiated power after 1871, meaning it wanted no more territory in Europe. He kept France isolated, and Germany's first colonies date only from 1884–85, so his policy was cautious and centred on Europe.
Wilhelm II forced Bismarck to resign in March 1890 (the resignation letter was dated 18 March and accepted on 20 March). This gives the contrast with Weltpolitik, the later policy of world ambitions.

Britain was an island empire that depended on sea trade and imported food, so it treated naval supremacy as a matter of survival. The two-power standard, set by the Naval Defence Act of 1889, required the Royal Navy to be at least equal to the next two largest navies combined.
Britain stayed out of alliances in a policy called splendid isolation, and its first peacetime alliance of this era was with Japan in January 1902.
Europe was already divided into two blocs: the Triple Alliance of 1882 (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Franco-Russian alliance (a military convention in 1892, an alliance in 1894).

Naval terms: a battleship (or capital ship) is the heaviest warship and a cruiser is lighter and faster. A battle fleet is built to fight a decisive battle in home waters, whereas a cruiser fleet protects trade and colonies overseas.
notes.tip: If a question asks why Britain reacted so strongly to the German fleet, link it to Britain's dependence on sea power and to the fleet's position in the North Sea.

notes.h: Key personality: Wilhelm II, family, character and accession
notes.b: Wilhelm II was Kaiser from 1888 to 1918. His family ties, his disability and his restless temperament shaped how he ruled and why he loved the navy.
points: He was born in Berlin on 27 January 1859, the eldest son of Crown Prince Frederick (later Frederick III) and Victoria, the eldest daughter of Queen Victoria, which made him her grandson. A breech birth damaged his left arm, which stayed withered and shorter.
1888 was the year of the three emperors. Wilhelm I died on 9 March, Frederick III reigned 99 days and died on 15 June, and Wilhelm II became Kaiser that day, aged 29.
Do not confuse the three rulers: Wilhelm I was Kaiser from 1871 to 1888, Frederick III only in 1888, and Wilhelm II from 1888 to 1918.
He was energetic, intelligent, impulsive, theatrical, militaristic and easily influenced, so his enthusiasms could swing quickly and his public words often embarrassed his ministers.

His feelings about Britain mixed love and hate. George V and Tsarina Alexandra (the wife of Nicholas II) were his first cousins, and Nicholas II was a more distant relative, while he admired the Royal Navy but resented British power.
His passion for the navy was long-standing: Queen Victoria made him an honorary Admiral of the Fleet of the Royal Navy in 1889, and he attended the Spithead naval review that year.

Contemporaries were divided. Nationalists and navalists admired him as the symbol of Germany's rise, abroad he was regarded as erratic and a threat (foreign cartoonists drew him as a menace), and after 1908 he was criticised at home too.
notes.tip: Do not call Nicholas II his first cousin. George V and Tsarina Alexandra were; Nicholas II was only a more distant relative.

notes.h: Key personality: Wilhelm II, Bismarck and the new course
notes.b: Wilhelm wanted to rule himself, which made a clash with the old Chancellor almost certain. After Bismarck went, a new course under Chancellor Caprivi changed German policy at home and abroad.
points: Wilhelm's aim was personal rule (Persönliches Regiment): to govern himself rather than through a strong Chancellor. He forced Bismarck to resign in March 1890, a moment Punch marked with John Tenniel's cartoon "Dropping the Pilot".
How far he really achieved personal rule is debated, because the Reichstag held the budget and his own changeable moods undermined his control.
His Chancellors were Caprivi (1890–94), Prince Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst (1894–1900), Bernhard von Bülow (1900–09) and Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg (1909–17).

The new course (Neuer Kurs) was Caprivi's policy of 1890–94, not Weltpolitik. Abroad, the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia was not renewed in 1890, and the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty with Britain (1 July 1890) gave Germany Heligoland and Britain Zanzibar.
At home Wilhelm began by easing the Anti-Socialist Law, which lapsed on 30 September 1890, and sponsored the workers' protection law of 1891 (Sunday rest, limits on child and women's labour).
Caprivi's trade treaties of 1891–94 lowered tariffs on grain, which angered the agrarians (the landowners who wanted grain protected from foreign competition).
The SPD kept growing, so Wilhelm then turned against it, and Caprivi fell in 1894.
notes.tip: For essays comparing Bismarck and Wilhelm II, the lapse of the Reinsurance Treaty in 1890 is the turning point. Give dates for both men, contrast Bismarck's caution with Weltpolitik's provocation, and reach a verdict.

notes.h: Key personality: Wilhelm II, indiscretions and personal diplomacy
notes.b: Wilhelm liked to act as his own diplomat, but his impulsive words and private deals repeatedly damaged Germany's image. Three separate indiscretions, and one failed treaty, show the pattern.
points: First came the Kruger telegram of 3 January 1896, which angered British opinion because it congratulated the Boer president on defeating the Jameson Raid into the Transvaal.

Second was the Hun speech, given on 27 July 1900 to troops leaving Bremerhaven for China. He told them to give no quarter and to make the name German feared as the Huns had made theirs, which damaged Germany's image abroad.

Third was the Daily Telegraph interview, published on 28 October 1908. He said most Germans were hostile to Britain but that he was its friend, and claimed he had sent Queen Victoria a plan for the Boer War.
He also said the fleet was aimed at the Far East, which offended Japan as well as Britain.

There was uproar in the Reichstag and press across all parties. Bülow did not defend him, Wilhelm promised in November 1908 to respect his constitutional responsibilities, and he suffered a nervous collapse. He then withdrew from many public roles.
He never fully trusted Bülow again, and Bülow resigned in July 1909. The direct cause was the defeat of his finance reform, but the loss of the Kaiser's trust meant he had no support to carry on.
Wilhelm also practised personal diplomacy through the Willy-Nicky letters and telegrams, written in English, to Nicholas II.

In July 1905 the two men signed the Treaty of Björkö, a defensive alliance, on Nicholas's yacht. It was never put into effect because the Russian government and Bülow objected, which shows how limited personal diplomacy was.
notes.tip: Keep the three indiscretions apart: the Kruger telegram (1896), the Hun speech (1900) and the Daily Telegraph affair (1908). Name them rather than quoting them, and do not present the Telegraph affair as the direct cause of Bülow's fall.

notes.h: Key personality: Wilhelm II, 1912, war and judgements
notes.b: Wilhelm's last years of real influence run from the war council of 1912 to defeat in 1918. Historians still argue about how far he controlled events and how much blame he carries.
points: On 8 December 1912 Wilhelm met his army and navy chiefs, Moltke and Tirpitz, without the Chancellor, after a British warning that Britain would not stand aside if France were attacked.

Moltke said war the sooner the better, Tirpitz asked for more time for the navy, and no decision for war was recorded. Röhl and Fischer's followers treat the meeting as evidence of planning, while others, such as Clark, see bellicose talk without consequence.
In July 1914 he gave Austria-Hungary the blank cheque (5–6 July). There is more on this in the notes on Serbia and the outbreak of war; in wartime his role declined as the generals took over.

He lost the army's confidence in autumn 1918. Chancellor Prince Max of Baden announced his abdication in Berlin on 9 November 1918, he crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November, and he abdicated formally on 28 November.
He lived at Doorn in the Netherlands from 1920 and died there on 4 June 1941.

He was a participant, not a bystander: he chose Tirpitz and Bülow and backed the fleet throughout. Yet he worked within pressures from nationalist groups, industry and the military, so he both shaped events and was shaped by them.
John Röhl (a three-volume biography, 1993–2008) argues that Wilhelm exercised genuine personal rule and bears heavy responsibility for 1914.

Christopher Clark (Kaiser Wilhelm II, 2000, and The Sleepwalkers, 2012) portrays him as erratic and often sidelined, with responsibility shared among all the Great Powers, while Fritz Fischer's school places German leadership at the centre of 1914.
notes.tip: On how much Wilhelm really ruled, set Röhl against Clark and give each historian's argument. Examiners want the contrast, not just one view.

notes.b: Weltpolitik, meaning world policy, was the attempt to turn Germany from a European power into a world power. It grew from economic need, domestic politics and national pride.
points: Weltpolitik was the attempt from about 1897 to make Germany a world power through colonies, trade, influence and a battle fleet, as opposed to Bismarck's Europe-centred (continental) policy. It is usually dated from 1897, when Bülow and Tirpitz were appointed.
In January 1896, at the 25th anniversary of the Reich, Wilhelm said the German Empire had become a world empire. In 1898 at Stettin he declared "Our future lies on the water."

Economic causes: by 1900 Germany had overtaken Britain in steel production, and by 1914 its merchant fleet was second only to Britain's. A growing industry needed markets, raw materials and secure sea routes, and feared being shut out as Britain, France and Russia expanded.

Sammlungspolitik (the politics of rallying together), associated with Johannes von Miquel, the Prussian finance minister, from 1897, aimed to unite industrialists, landowners and the middle classes behind the monarchy and against the SPD.

Social imperialism is a historians' term, used by Wehler and others, for using overseas expansion to divert domestic discontent. Conservatives and many liberals hoped imperial success would unite the classes behind the monarchy and distract from the SPD.
Pressure groups pushed the policy: the Colonial Society (founded 1887), the Pan-German League (founded 1891, named the Pan-German League from 1894) and the German Navy League (founded April 1898).

Nationalism in Germany meant pride in the new Reich and a belief that a great nation needed colonies, world influence and a fleet. Germany felt late to empire and resented the empires of Britain and France.
Social Darwinist ideas (that nations compete like species and only the strong survive) made rivalry between nations seem natural.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Weltpolitik with the new course: the new course was Caprivi's policy of 1890–94, and Weltpolitik began about 1897.

notes.h: Weltpolitik in action: Bülow, Africa, China, the Pacific and the Ottoman Empire
notes.b: Weltpolitik was carried out through a series of moves between 1896 and 1903. Each gave Germany little, but each alarmed another power.
points: Bernhard von Bülow was appointed Foreign Secretary in June 1897 (formally in October) and was Chancellor from 17 October 1900 to July 1909. In his Reichstag speech of 6 December 1897 he said Germany wanted to put no one in the shade but demanded "a place in the sun".

On 3 January 1896 Wilhelm sent the Kruger telegram, congratulating President Paul Kruger of the Transvaal on defeating the Jameson Raid (29 December 1895 to 2 January 1896) without appealing to the help of friendly powers, as it was reported. British press and public were outraged.

Two German Catholic missionaries were murdered in Shandong province, China, on 1 November 1897. German ships seized Kiaochow Bay, with the port of Tsingtao, that month, and a 99-year lease was signed in March 1898.

In the Boxer rising of 1900 the German minister in Peking, Baron von Ketteler, was killed in June. Field Marshal von Waldersee commanded the international relief force, which arrived after Peking had already been relieved.

In 1899 Germany bought the Caroline, Mariana (except Guam) and Palau islands from Spain. Samoa was partitioned that year between Germany and the USA, with Britain withdrawing in return for compensation elsewhere.
In October and November 1898 Wilhelm toured the Ottoman Empire (Constantinople, Jerusalem and Damascus), and at Damascus he declared himself the friend of the world's Muslims.

The Baghdad Railway had a preliminary concession in 1899 and a full convention in 1903. It was meant to tie the Ottoman Empire to Germany and rival British and Russian influence in the Middle East, so both powers were suspicious; it was still unfinished in 1914.
notes.tip: Examiners reward linking each episode to its effect on a named power: the Kruger telegram on Britain, the Baghdad Railway on Russia and Britain, Morocco on France. Never attribute a place in the sun to Wilhelm; it was Bülow's phrase.

notes.h: Weltpolitik and the balance of power
notes.b: The balance of power means that no single state or bloc is strong enough to dominate. Weltpolitik brought Germany small gains but alarmed every other power, so it weakened Germany's own position.
points: Britain had traditionally opposed any power dominating the Continent and treated naval supremacy as its own security. Germany's growing power, and later its fleet, threatened both, which pushed Britain towards France and Russia.

Talks between Joseph Chamberlain, the British Colonial Secretary, and Germany in 1898–1901 for an Anglo-German alliance came to nothing. Bülow and Holstein thought Britain would have to pay a higher price later, so they did not press for agreement.
Britain then turned to Japan (the alliance of January 1902) and France (the Entente Cordiale of April 1904) instead.

Wilhelm's visit to Tangier on 31 March 1905 began the first Moroccan crisis. At the Algeciras Conference of 1906 Germany was isolated, backed only by Austria-Hungary, so the result was humiliation and a stronger Entente.

In July 1911 Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir, Morocco. After Lloyd George's Mansion House speech (July 1911) warned Germany, it accepted part of the French Congo in November 1911 in return for recognising French control of Morocco.
Germans came to believe that Britain, France and Russia were hemming Germany in, a belief called Einkreisung (encirclement). Critics say German policy itself caused it.

In short, Germany's gains were small, but it alarmed every other power, pushed Britain into the Entente and left Germany relying on Austria-Hungary. There is more on the Moroccan crises in the notes on colonial rivalries.
notes.tip: On how far Weltpolitik damaged international relations, finish with a verdict on the balance of power. Do not call Tangier itself a defeat; the humiliation came at Algeciras in 1906.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: background and causes
notes.b: Before 1897 Germany's strength lay in its army and its navy was small. The decision to build a great battle fleet, taken in 1897-98, came from the Kaiser's enthusiasm, a book on sea power and a determined admiral.
points: Before 1897 the German navy was small and largely a coastal defence force, and its earlier leaders favoured cruisers. Germany's strength was its army.

Wilhelm was personally enthusiastic about a navy to rival Britain's. He admired the Royal Navy (he was an honorary British admiral from 1889 and attended the Spithead review that year) and wanted a fleet that matched Germany's new status.

Alfred Thayer Mahan, a US naval officer, argued in The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890) that national greatness depended on a strong battle fleet and command of the sea. Wilhelm said he was devouring it and had copies placed on his warships.

Alfred von Tirpitz was appointed State Secretary of the Imperial Navy Office (Reichsmarineamt) in June 1897 and held the post until March 1916. His memorandum of June 1897 named Britain as the most dangerous naval enemy.

He called for a battle fleet concentrated in the North Sea, aimed in practice at Britain, rather than a cruiser fleet for overseas, because only a fleet in home waters could threaten the Royal Navy where it was most vulnerable.
Wilhelm chose Tirpitz and backed the fleet throughout, so the Kaiser's enthusiasm and the admiral's plan reinforced each other.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the reasons Germany built a fleet: prestige, Mahan, trade and colonies, domestic politics, Wilhelm's personality and the risk theory. Each accurate dated statement counts, such as Mahan (1890) and Tirpitz (1897).

notes.h: Naval policy case study: the risk theory and the aims behind the fleet
notes.b: Tirpitz needed a reason why a smaller fleet could still work, and reasons at home to win Reichstag money. His risk theory and his domestic aims explain how the fleet was designed and sold.
points: The risk theory (Risikogedanke) held that the fleet need not beat the Royal Navy, only be strong enough that a battle would cost Britain so much that it would be left exposed to other powers, France and Russia. Britain would therefore avoid war and treat Germany as an equal.

Tirpitz's target is often given as a ratio of about 2:3 against Britain, which the Kaiser and Tirpitz judged enough to make the theory work. He also hoped the fleet would win an alliance or colonial concessions from Britain.
The danger zone was the building period, when Britain might strike first before the fleet was strong enough. Germans feared a Copenhagen, after Britain's seizure of the Danish fleet in 1807.
The fleet was also a national project to rally the middle classes behind the Reich and isolate the SPD, an example of Sammlungspolitik and social imperialism.
The Navy Laws fixed the size of the fleet and the replacement of ships in law, so later Reichstags had to fund them and could not easily cut the programme.
The Navy Office's News Bureau organised press and lecture campaigns, and academic supporters who lectured and wrote for the fleet were called Flottenprofessoren (fleet professors).
The German Navy League (Deutscher Flottenverein), founded in April 1898 and funded in part by industrialists including Krupp, was a mass organisation promoting the fleet.
Industry gained from the programme: Krupp of Essen supplied armour plate and guns, and Blohm & Voss of Hamburg built warships, so heavy industry gained orders.
notes.tip: Be able to state the risk theory and its aim. Do not claim the Navy League had over a million members; the figure is unreliable, so call it a mass organisation.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: the Navy Laws and Britain's first response
notes.b: Germany turned the plan into law in 1898 and 1900. Britain at first reacted by reorganising its fleet rather than racing.
points: The First Navy Law, passed by the Reichstag on 26 March 1898, provided for 19 battleships, with cruisers and coastal armoured ships, to be built by 1904. Spending was fixed in law up to 1904.
The Second Navy Law (June 1900) doubled the battleship target to 38, to be reached over about twenty years, plus more cruisers.

German anger helped pass it. From late December 1899 to January 1900 the Royal Navy stopped and searched German mail steamers (Bundesrath, Herzog and General) off south-east Africa, suspecting contraband for the Boers during the Boer War.
The Bundesrath was stopped off Delagoa Bay on 29 December 1899, so the outrage that helped the Second Navy Law was German anger at Britain, not British anger at Germany.

The Admiralty's attention turned increasingly to Germany. Sir John Fisher, First Sea Lord from October 1904 to 1910, scrapped many obsolete ships, brought warships home from distant stations and concentrated them to face the North Sea, and British naval estimates grew.
Fisher's redeployment in 1904–05 was possible because the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902 let Britain reduce its Far East fleet and the Entente Cordiale of 1904 settled disputes with France.

Invasion-scare literature spread British alarm: Erskine Childers's novel The Riddle of the Sands (1903) about a German invasion plan, and William Le Queux's The Invasion of 1910 (1906), serialised in the Daily Mail. A British Navy League had existed since 1894.
notes.tip: The Second Navy Law was passed amid German anger at the stopping of German mail steamers, not British anger over the Boer War. Giving it as British anger is a common mistake.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: the Dreadnought, the German response and the 1909 scare
notes.b: In 1906 a new British ship changed the race. Germany answered with more building, and by 1909 the race had become a public scare in Britain.
points: HMS Dreadnought was launched at Portsmouth on 10 February 1906 by Edward VII and completed in December 1906. She carried ten 12-inch guns, had steam turbines and reached a speed of about 21 knots.

Dreadnought became the name for all battleships of her type, and pre-dreadnought for older ones, which she made obsolete. This cut Britain's existing lead but also gave Germany a chance to compete on equal terms.
However, Britain still had a head start in building dreadnoughts and a far larger fleet overall, so the Dreadnought did not put Germany level with Britain.

Germany answered with its own dreadnoughts. SMS Nassau, its first, was launched in March 1908. The supplementary law (Novelle) of 1906 added large cruisers and provided for widening the Kiel Canal so that dreadnoughts could use it.
The 1908 law cut the life of a battleship from 25 to 20 years, so Germany would build four capital ships a year for 1908–11. The widened Kiel Canal reopened in June 1914.
In 1908–09 a naval scare broke out in Britain over fears that Germany was building faster than announced. The public demanded eight new dreadnoughts with the slogan "We want eight and we won't wait."

Asquith's Liberal government, with Reginald McKenna as First Lord of the Admiralty, agreed to eight dreadnoughts in the 1909–10 programme (four at once, four more later). Britain had decided to out-build Germany at any cost.
Lloyd George's 1909 People's Budget had to pay for both the navy and social reform, so the race strained Britain's finances too.
notes.tip: When you mention the Dreadnought, add that it made older battleships obsolete but that Britain kept a head start in dreadnoughts and a far larger fleet. Dated laws (1898, 1900, 1908, 1912) and the Dreadnought (1906) are the expected evidence.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: failed talks, the Haldane mission and the end of the race
notes.b: Both governments tried to talk their way out of the race, but each wanted the other to move first. After 1912 Germany gave up the race in practice.
points: Britain proposed arms limitation at the Second Hague Conference (1907), but Germany refused to discuss it. In the talks of 1906-08 and up to 1911, Germany wanted a British neutrality promise before limiting building, while Britain wanted limits first.
Bethmann Hollweg, Chancellor from July 1909, sought a naval and political agreement in 1909–11 but none was reached.

Richard Haldane, British Secretary of State for War, visited Berlin on 8–11 February 1912, arranged through the shipping magnate Albert Ballin and the banker Sir Ernest Cassel. Germany asked for a pledge of British neutrality if Germany became involved in a war.

Britain would promise only not to join an unprovoked attack on Germany, and wanted building slowed first. Neutrality would have left France and Russia to face Germany alone. Wilhelm also announced a new Navy Law in his Reichstag speech of 7 February 1912, just as the mission began.

The 1912 supplementary law added three more battleships and a third active battle squadron. Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty from October 1911 to May 1915, told the Commons in March 1912 that Britain would keep a 60 per cent superiority in dreadnoughts over Germany.

Churchill proposed a naval holiday (a pause in building) in 1912 and again in 1913, but Germany did not accept. In 1912 British battleships moved from the Mediterranean to home waters while France concentrated its fleet in the Mediterranean; the Grey-Cambon letters (November 1912) promised consultation, not alliance.

From 1912–13 Germany shifted money to the army, which received large increases in 1912 and 1913. In 1913 Tirpitz told the Reichstag budget committee that Germany accepted a 16:10 ratio in battleships in Britain's favour, and in August 1914 Britain had a clear lead in dreadnoughts.

A limited detente followed in 1913–14: an agreement on the future of the Portuguese colonies was initialled in 1913 and a Baghdad Railway agreement in June 1914. Mistrust remained, and the naval and military preparations of each side continued.
notes.tip: To explain why talks failed, state the deadlock: Germany wanted a British neutrality pledge before limiting building, and Britain wanted limits first. The Haldane mission of 1912 is expected evidence.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: outcomes for Germany at home
notes.b: The fleet failed to achieve its aims abroad and it also cost Germany heavily at home. The money problem fed straight into party politics.
points: The fleet cost vast sums and absorbed resources that could have gone to the army, at a time when Germany's land frontiers were threatened by France and Russia. The navy took a growing share of the defence budget until 1912.
Rising naval spending raised the national debt and taxation and led to the Reich finance crisis of 1908–09.

In June 1909 Bülow's finance reform, which included an inheritance tax, was defeated in the Reichstag by the Conservatives and the Centre Party. Bülow resigned in July 1909, having lost the Kaiser's trust.
The dispute sharpened the quarrel between the Conservatives, who opposed the inheritance tax, and the left. The SPD and left-liberals also opposed the cost of the fleet.
The fleet rallied the right for a time, but it did not halt the SPD's growth: in the January 1912 Reichstag election the SPD won 110 seats and became the largest party.
After 1912 Germany could no longer afford to compete in both navy and army, so the army received large increases in 1912–13 and the naval race slackened.
notes.tip: Essays on the problems naval policy caused for Germany and Europe need a judgement sustained throughout. Marshal the evidence: it alienated Britain, set off an arms race Germany could not win, strained finances (1908–09), took money from the army, failed its risk-theory aim and helped bring Britain into the war.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: outcomes for Britain, the war and the fleet
notes.b: The fleet failed in its main aim. It did not deter Britain; it turned a possible partner into an opponent, and in the war itself it achieved little.
points: The fleet turned a possible partner into an opponent. Britain's agreements with Japan (1902, which let it reduce its Far East fleet), France (1904, settling Egypt and Morocco) and Russia (1907, covering Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet) formed, with the Franco-Russian alliance, the Triple Entente.
Historians debate how far the navy, rather than colonial issues, caused these agreements. The 1904 Entente was mainly a colonial settlement, so the navy's role is disputed.

The fleet did not deter Britain. It helped make Britain regard Germany as the main threat and bound Britain more closely to France, so Britain declared war on 4 August 1914, after Germany invaded Belgium. There is more on this in the notes on Serbia and the outbreak of war.

In the war the navy stayed mostly in harbour. At Jutland (31 May-1 June 1916) Britain lost more ships and men, about 6,000 British and about 2,500 German dead, but the German High Seas Fleet returned to port and rarely came out again, and the British blockade was never broken.

Many sailors resented the fleet's inactivity and harsh discipline. The mutinies at Wilhelmshaven (late October 1918) and Kiel (from 3 November 1918) helped start the revolution that overthrew the Kaiser.
The interned German fleet was scuttled at Scapa Flow on 21 June 1919 on the orders of Admiral Ludwig von Reuter.
notes.tip: Explain why the fleet failed its own aim: Britain was not deterred, out-built Germany and made friends with its rivals. Remember that Belgium was the immediate trigger for Britain's entry in 1914, and the navy was the deeper cause.

notes.h: Naval policy case study: significance and contemporary views
notes.b: People at the time judged the fleet very differently depending on where they stood. A document question will often turn on spotting the writer's side.
points: British contemporaries regarded the German fleet as a challenge to the Empire. The Admiralty, the public and the press spread alarm, including invasion scares and the Daily Mail, and the British Navy League added to it.
German nationalists were proud of the fleet and presented it as essential for the defence of overseas trade, and they explained Britain's hostility through the encirclement view.
The SPD and left-liberals objected to the cost of the fleet.
The two nations' views were mirror images: Germany saw a peaceful trading nation needing protection, Britain saw a fleet in the North Sea aimed at itself.
notes.tip: In document questions, identify each writer's view (Germany as a peaceful trading nation needing protection against British fear of a fleet in the North Sea) and add one outside fact, such as the Dreadnought (1906).

notes.h: Naval policy case study: how historians judge the fleet
notes.b: Historians disagree about why Germany built the fleet and what it caused. Match each historian to a clear view.
points: Eckart Kehr (Battleship Building and Party Politics, German 1930) argued that the fleet served the domestic interests of industry and the middle classes, a view known as the primacy of domestic politics (Primat der Innenpolitik).

Volker Berghahn (Der Tirpitz-Plan, 1971) argued that Tirpitz aimed to strengthen the monarchy against the Reichstag and to deter or blackmail Britain. Social imperialism is a term associated mainly with Wehler, not with Berghahn.

Fritz Fischer (Griff nach der Weltmacht, 1961; in English Germany's Aims in the First World War, 1967) and War of Illusions (German 1969) argued that Germany's leaders deliberately sought world power, first by the fleet and then by war. Critics say he exaggerated the coherence of German aims.

Paul Kennedy (The Rise of the Anglo-German Antagonism, 1860–1914, 1980) argues that the naval race was central to the breakdown of Anglo-German relations, though rooted in wider economic and political rivalry.
Niall Ferguson (The Pity of War, 1998) argues that Britain had clearly won the naval race by about 1912, so it was not a direct cause of war in 1914.
Other historians doubt that the race caused the war, because Anglo-German relations were improving in 1913–14 and the Entente was formed first because of colonial concerns.
notes.tip: Name at least one historian with a view and match it correctly: Kehr and Berghahn for domestic motives, Fischer for a deliberate drive for world power, Kennedy for the race as central to antagonism, Ferguson for Britain having won by about 1912.

notes.h: Assessment: Weltpolitik and the naval race
notes.b: A judgement answer needs achievements set against limits. These paired points give the balance examiners reward.
points: Achievement: Germany built the world's second-largest navy in under two decades, winning national pride and support for the Kaiser.
Limit: the fleet never came near matching Britain, and the risk theory failed because Britain out-built Germany and made friends with its rivals.
Achievement: Weltpolitik won Kiaochow, the Pacific islands, Samoa and the Baghdad Railway concession, and gave Germany a voice in world affairs.
Limit: the gains were small and unprofitable, the Morocco crises ended in humiliation, and Germany became more isolated, relying on Austria-Hungary.
Domestic achievement: the fleet and the colonial movement helped rally the right for a time, bringing Conservatives and National Liberals together behind the government.
Domestic limit: its cost caused the 1908–09 finance crisis and did not halt the SPD's growth, since the SPD became the largest party in 1912.
Contemporary view: German contemporaries regarded Weltpolitik and the fleet as a necessary national project, while British contemporaries regarded them as a direct threat.

Later view: most historians judge Weltpolitik and the fleet a strategic mistake that helped make the Triple Entente and brought Britain into the war, though some stress that Anglo-German relations were improving by 1914.
notes.tip: Judgement points are rewarded as pairs: second-largest navy against never close to Britain, colonies gained against small and costly, domestic rallying against finance crisis and SPD growth. Name a historian and a contemporary view.

keyTerms.definition: German 'world policy' from the late 1890s: a drive for colonies, trade, a large navy and an equal place among the world powers.
A situation in which no one state can dominate Europe because rivals combine to check it; Germany's naval ambition disturbed it.
Pride in and loyalty to one's nation; in Germany it drove support for the navy through bodies such as the Navy League.
Tirpitz's argument that a fleet strong enough to damage the Royal Navy would deter Britain from war with Germany.
The all-big-gun battleship launched by Britain in 1906, which made earlier battleships obsolete and began a new phase of the naval race.
The British rule, from the Naval Defence Act of 1889, that the Royal Navy should equal the next two largest navies combined.
The German Flottenverein, founded in 1898, a mass pressure group that campaigned for a bigger navy.
The German fear, strong before 1914, that France, Russia and Britain were hemming Germany in.

factCards.term: What did the First Navy Law of 1898 authorise?
factCards.definition: A fleet of 19 battleships, 8 large cruisers and 12 small cruisers.

factCards.term: What did the Second Navy Law of 1900 authorise?
factCards.definition: A fleet of 38 battleships and 20 large cruisers, passed amid anger in Germany over British action in the Boer War.
State secretary of the Imperial Navy Office from June 1897, architect of the German battle fleet and of the risk theory.

factCards.term: When was HMS Dreadnought launched, and why did it matter?
factCards.definition: On 10 February 1906; it was faster and more heavily armed than any existing battleship, so it made them obsolete and restarted the race.
A British minister's visit to Berlin in February 1912 to seek a naval agreement; it failed over Germany's demand for a British neutrality pledge.

factCards.term: Which book influenced German naval thinking?
factCards.definition: Alfred Thayer Mahan's The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890).

factCards.term: What was the 'We want eight' campaign?
factCards.definition: A 1909 British press and public campaign demanding eight new dreadnoughts in response to German building.

factCards.term: What was the Daily Telegraph affair?
factCards.definition: Wilhelm II's interview of October 1908, in which he made remarks offensive to Britain and others; it caused a constitutional crisis in Germany.
The only major fleet battle of the war, fought 31 May 1916 and indecisive; the German fleet stayed largely in port afterwards.

factCards.term: How do historians assess Wilhelm II?
factCards.definition: Röhl stresses his personal rule and responsibility; Clark stresses his inconsistency and the shared responsibility of all the powers in 1914.
